didyouknow.t: An empty grave waits for Jesus in Medina
didyouknow.d: A long-standing tradition, resting on a report in Tirmidhi, holds that a burial spot in the Prophet's chamber in Medina — beside Muhammad, Abu Bakr, and Umar — is reserved for Jesus (Isa), who Muslims believe will return, live out a natural life, die, and be buried there. Mainstream Muslim media discuss the reserved spot matter-of-factly.

img.cap: The Green Dome over Muhammad's burial chamber, Medina

didyouknow.t: Jesus returns — to break the cross
didyouknow.d: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad says the son of Mary will descend as a just ruler, 'break the cross, kill the pigs, and abolish the jizya.' In Islamic eschatology Jesus returns not to vindicate Christianity but to end it — dismantling its central symbol and folding everyone into Islam.

didyouknow.t: The one-eyed false messiah
didyouknow.d: Muslims await the Dajjal, a one-eyed deceiver with 'kafir' (disbeliever) written between his eyes, whom every prophet warned about. He performs counterfeit miracles before Jesus descends and destroys him — a striking parallel to the Christian Antichrist.

didyouknow.t: The Mahdi: Islam's awaited deliverer
didyouknow.d: Sunnis await a yet-unborn descendant of Muhammad who will fill the earth with justice before the end; Twelver Shia believe he was born in the 9th century and has been alive in hiding (occultation) ever since. The Mahdi-Jesus-Dajjal drama forms a complete end-times narrative most Christians have never heard.

didyouknow.t: Jinn: a third order of beings
didyouknow.d: The Quran teaches God made angels from light, humans from clay, and jinn from 'smokeless fire' (55:15) — invisible beings who eat, marry, die, and will be judged. Solomon is said to have commanded armies of jinn as builders and divers (34:12-13), and belief in jinn possession remains live and mainstream.

didyouknow.t: The evil eye 'is real'
didyouknow.d: An authenticated hadith states 'the influence of an evil eye is a fact' — envious glances can cause real harm. This is why many Muslims say 'mashallah' when complimenting a baby, and why blue-eye amulets (culturally frowned on by scholars) blanket the Muslim world.

img.cap: Nazar amulets against the evil eye

didyouknow.t: Gabriel's six hundred wings
didyouknow.d: Muhammad is reported to have seen Gabriel in his true form with six hundred wings, filling the horizon. Gabriel (Jibril) holds a towering place in Islam as the sole conduit of the Quran, delivered piecemeal over 23 years.

didyouknow.t: Two angels ride your shoulders
didyouknow.d: The Kiraman Katibin ('noble scribes') sit on each person's right and left shoulders, recording every good and bad deed for the Day of Judgment (Quran 50:17-18; 82:10-12). Many Muslims end prayer by greeting both angels with a turn of the head.

didyouknow.t: Angels avoid homes with dogs or pictures
didyouknow.d: Per hadith, 'angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog or images' of living beings. This is why many observant Muslims won't keep dogs indoors (guard and working dogs excepted) and why some homes have no family photos on the walls.

didyouknow.t: Devils are chained during Ramadan
didyouknow.d: Muhammad taught that when Ramadan begins, 'the gates of heaven are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained.' It frames Ramadan as a month when sin is harder to blame on Satan — any evil done is your own nafs (self).

didyouknow.t: One night worth 83 years
didyouknow.d: Laylat al-Qadr, the night the Quran began descending, is 'better than a thousand months' (Quran 97:3) — worship that night outweighs 83+ years of it. Its exact date is hidden among the last ten odd nights of Ramadan, so devout Muslims pray through all of them.

didyouknow.t: The Kaaba gets a new $4-million dress yearly
didyouknow.d: The kiswa — the Kaaba's black silk cover embroidered with gold Quranic calligraphy — is replaced every year during Hajj. The old one is cut into pieces and gifted to dignitaries, museums, and organizations; fragments are treasured heirlooms.

img.cap: The kiswa — the Kaaba's embroidered cover

didyouknow.t: One family has held the Kaaba's key since Muhammad
didyouknow.d: The Bani Shaiba family has kept the key to the Kaaba since pre-Islamic times; Muhammad returned the key to them at the conquest of Mecca, and their descendants still open and clean the Kaaba today. Even Saudi kings must go through them to enter.

didyouknow.t: Zamzam: the well that hasn't run dry
didyouknow.d: Muslims trace the Zamzam well in Mecca to God's provision for Hagar and Ishmael — the same figures Genesis 21 places in the wilderness of Beersheba. It still pumps up to 18.5 liters per second for millions of pilgrims, who carry bottles of it home worldwide.

didyouknow.t: A winged steed and a night flight to Jerusalem
didyouknow.d: On the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj), Muhammad rode the Buraq from Mecca to Jerusalem, ascended through the heavens, met earlier prophets, and negotiated the daily prayers down from fifty to five — with Moses coaching the reductions. This event is why Jerusalem is Islam's third-holiest city.

img.cap: The Dome of the Rock — the Night Journey's destination

didyouknow.t: The 99 names of Allah
didyouknow.d: A hadith promises that whoever 'enumerates' Allah's ninety-nine names — the Merciful, the King, the Provider — will enter Paradise. Devout Muslims memorize them, count them on prayer beads, and name children with them (Abdul-Rahman = 'servant of the Merciful').

img.cap: A misbaha — beads for counting the names

didyouknow.t: The moon decides the holidays — and causes arguments
didyouknow.d: Islamic months begin at the sighted crescent moon, so Ramadan and Eid can start on different days in different countries — even neighboring ones — and Saudi announcements are regularly disputed by astronomers. 'Moon wars' are an annual, good-natured (and sometimes not) drama in Muslim communities.

didyouknow.t: Praying together multiplies the reward 27 times
didyouknow.d: Per hadith, congregational prayer is 'twenty-seven times superior' to praying alone — the engine behind mosque attendance. Worshippers also stand shoulder-to-shoulder in meticulously straight rows, because 'straightening the rows is part of the perfection of prayer.'

didyouknow.t: The first sound a Muslim baby hears
didyouknow.d: Following the practice of Muhammad with his grandson Hasan, the adhan (call to prayer) is whispered into a newborn's right ear so the first words the child hears are the declaration of God's oneness. Life begins and ends framed by the shahada.

didyouknow.t: Right hand, left hand — and a prayer for the bathroom
didyouknow.d: Islamic etiquette assigns the right hand to eating, drinking, and greeting, and the left to personal cleaning; there are prescribed supplications for entering the toilet (seeking refuge from devils) and leaving it ('Your forgiveness'). Daily life is scripted down to which foot enters a room first.

didyouknow.t: Prophetic medicine: the toothstick and the black seed
didyouknow.d: Muhammad said he would have commanded the miswak (teeth-cleaning twig) before every prayer were it not a burden, and that black seed is 'a cure for every disease except death' (Bukhari 5688). Both remain everyday items in Muslim homes, sold in every Islamic bookstore.

didyouknow.t: Why mosques are covered in writing, not pictures
didyouknow.d: Hadith literature warns image-makers of living beings will be challenged on Judgment Day to 'breathe life' into what they made, so Islamic sacred art avoids figures entirely. The result: calligraphy became Islam's highest art form — the word of God as decoration.

img.cap: Calligraphy in the Süleymaniye Mosque, Istanbul

didyouknow.t: A trillion-dollar interest-free economy
didyouknow.d: Because the Quran forbids riba (interest), a parallel global financial industry exists: Islamic banks, takaful insurance, and sukuk (sharia-compliant bonds) — a sukuk market now exceeding $1 trillion. Your Muslim neighbor may structure their mortgage, savings, and retirement around avoiding interest entirely.

didyouknow.t: Millions know the whole Quran by heart
didyouknow.d: A hafiz has memorized the entire Quran — roughly 600 pages of classical Arabic — and millions worldwide have done it, most of them non-Arabic speakers; Pakistan alone certifies tens of thousands of new huffaz every year. No comparable memorization culture exists for any other book.

didyouknow.t: Islam's oldest monument is an anti-Trinitarian argument
didyouknow.d: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (built 72 AH / 691-92 by caliph Abd al-Malik) carries the earliest monumental Islamic inscriptions in existence — and they are a direct polemic against Christian doctrine. The 240-meter mosaic band inside quotes and paraphrases Quran 4:171 and 19:35: 'Do not say Three... God is only one God; far be it from His glory that He should have a son.' Before Islam had minted its classic law books or collected its hadith, it was already defining itself against the Trinity — on Jerusalem's skyline, facing the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The oldest physical Islamic proclamation is a denial of the Sonship of Christ.

didyouknow.t: The computer 'miracle' that ended in a murder
didyouknow.d: In the 1970s-80s, Egyptian-American biochemist Rashad Khalifa announced a computer-discovered 'mathematical miracle': the Quran's structure was built on the number 19 (from Quran 74:30). The catch: his counts only worked after he removed two verses (9:128-129) from the Quran as 'satanic insertions.' He went on to declare himself God's 'Messenger of the Covenant.' Mainstream scholars condemned him as an apostate, and on January 31, 1990 he was stabbed to death in his Tucson mosque; his killer was convicted in 2013. The episode is a case study in what happens when a 'proof' of the Quran requires editing the Quran — and in how heresy is policed.

didyouknow.t: Ashura: the wound that defines the Sunni-Shia split
didyouknow.d: Every year on 10 Muharram, Shia Muslims mourn the death of Husayn — Muhammad's grandson — killed with his family at Karbala (in modern Iraq) in 680 AD by the army of the caliph Yazid. Mourning processions include chest-beating, weeping majalis (lament gatherings), and in some communities self-flagellation with chains or blades (tatbir), though many Shia authorities now discourage blood rites and urge blood donation instead. Sunnis, by contrast, mark Ashura with an optional fast. That one day carries the whole Sunni-Shia divide in miniature: for Shia Islam, sacred history is a story of the Prophet's family betrayed by the Muslim community itself.

week.t: Five prayers that move with the sun
week.d: Salah happens at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, and night — times set by the sun's position, so fajr can mean a 4 a.m. alarm in summer and maghrib lands mid-commute in winter. Observant Muslims arrange work breaks, find quiet rooms, and sometimes combine prayers when traveling.
week.tip: If a Muslim colleague or friend disappears for ten minutes in the afternoon, that's prayer — treating it as normal (or offering a quiet room) builds more trust than a hundred arguments.

week.d: Prayer requires ritual purity — washing hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, and feet. It's why you may see someone washing their feet in an office restroom sink; certain things (sleep, using the toilet) break wudu and require redoing it.
week.tip: Don't react awkwardly to the restroom ritual; knowing the word 'wudu' and why it matters signals real respect.

week.d: Friday midday prayer at the mosque — a sermon (khutbah) plus short congregational prayer — is obligatory for men and is the Muslim week's center of gravity, like Sunday morning for churchgoers. Muhammad called Friday the best day the sun rises on.
week.tip: Never schedule something important with a Muslim friend for Friday early afternoon — and asking 'how was jummah?' lands like someone asking you about Sunday's sermon.

week.d: Beyond avoiding pork and alcohol, observant Muslims screen for hidden ingredients: pork gelatin in candy and marshmallows, wine in sauces, alcohol-based vanilla, animal rennet in cheese, and cross-contaminated fryers. Eating at a non-Muslim home is permitted — but only if they can trust what's in the food.
week.tip: When hosting, name your ingredients unprompted and serve fish or vegetarian; never assume 'the wine cooks off' solves it — for many it doesn't.

week.t: Ramadan: a month that rearranges life
week.d: For one lunar month, no food or water from first light to sunset: a pre-dawn meal (suhoor, 'in which there is blessing' per Bukhari), the sunset fast-breaking (iftar, traditionally with dates), and long taraweeh prayers at the mosque each night. The last ten nights are the most intense, as Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr; globally, dates sales and food markets surge around it.
week.tip: During Ramadan, don't invite them to lunch — offer to join them for iftar instead; being asked to share that meal is an honor.

week.d: Eid al-Fitr celebrates Ramadan's end; Eid al-Adha commemorates Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son (Muslims believe it was Ishmael) and coincides with Hajj — families gather, kids get gifts and new clothes, and it's the Muslim world's biggest shopping and feasting season. Muslims often take these days off work or pull kids from school.
week.tip: Learn the dates and say 'Eid Mubarak' — silence on Eid feels to them like a friend ignoring your Christmas.

week.t: Zakat: charity as a pillar, not a plate
week.d: Once wealth passes a threshold (nisab, ~85g of gold), an observant Muslim gives 2.5% of accumulated savings annually — a calculated obligation, not spontaneous giving, often paid during Ramadan for extra reward. Many treat the calculation as seriously as taxes.
week.tip: Generosity is deep common ground — comparing zakat and Christian giving is an easy, warm conversation that goes theological fast.

week.d: Hijab practice ranges from none to headscarf to full covering, by conviction, family, and culture — and modesty rules also govern gender interaction: many observant Muslims avoid being alone with, or touching, unrelated members of the opposite sex.
week.tip: Let the other person initiate a handshake across genders; a hand on the heart with a smile is a graceful, well-understood alternative.

week.d: Inshallah ('if God wills') accompanies any future plan; alhamdulillah ('praise be to God') answers 'how are you?' and follows sneezes and meals; astaghfirullah ('I seek God's forgiveness') responds to sin or shock; mashallah wards envy off anything praised. These signal continuous God-consciousness, not empty filler.
week.tip: Using inshallah and alhamdulillah sincerely (not performatively) is welcomed, and hearing them tells you where your friend's reflexes are — a Christian's 'Lord willing' (James 4:15) is a perfect bridge.

week.d: Sunni Islam has no ordained clergy or hierarchy — an imam is simply a knowledgeable man who leads prayer, hired and fired by the mosque community; he hears no confessions and dispenses no sacraments. The mosque functions as prayer hall, weekend school, and community hub.
week.tip: Don't map 'pastor' onto 'imam' — your friend's religious authority is diffuse (scholars, family, websites like IslamQA), so persuading one leader never moves a community.

week.d: Every able Muslim must make pilgrimage to Mecca once; families save for decades, and completing it confers the honored title 'Hajji' and, per hadith, a clean slate of sins. It's a bucket-list obligation with real financial planning behind it — often thousands of dollars per person.
week.tip: Asking 'have you been on Hajj — do you hope to go?' opens one of the most heartfelt conversations a Muslim can have, straight into what forgiveness costs.

week.d: Most observant families send children to weekend or after-school madrasa/maktab classes to learn Arabic recitation, memorization, and basics of the faith — some aiming for full hifz (memorizing all ~600 pages). Quran recitation competitions are the Muslim world's spelling bees.
week.tip: Ask parents what their kids are memorizing — pride in a child's Quran progress is universal, and it shows you why 'just read the Bible for yourself' lands differently in a memorization-first culture.

week.t: Cultural Muslims outnumber devout ones in many places
week.d: Practice varies enormously: 42% of U.S. Muslims say they pray all five daily prayers, while others observe only Ramadan and Eids — like Christmas-and-Easter Christians. Ethnic identity, family honor, and faith are braided together, so 'Muslim' may describe heritage more than conviction.
week.tip: Ask, don't assume — 'what does your faith look like day to day?' respects the person in front of you instead of the stereotype, and many nominal Muslims have never been asked.

aboutyou.t: Your worship of Jesus looks like the one unforgivable sin
aboutyou.d: Quran 4:48 teaches Allah may forgive anything except shirk — associating partners with God — and worshiping Jesus is the textbook example Muslims are taught. To your friend, the cross around your neck isn't neutral; it represents the sin that, if you die in it, God will not pardon.
aboutyou.tip: Lead with your monotheism: 'I believe in one God — let me tell you what I actually mean' must come before any 'Son of God' language, or you'll be filed under polytheist before you finish the sentence.

aboutyou.t: They think your Trinity includes Mary
aboutyou.d: In Quran 5:116, God asks Jesus whether he told people to 'take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah' — so many Muslims grow up assuming the Trinity is Father, Jesus, and Mary, and that Christians worship three gods. Their objections often target this version, not what you believe.
aboutyou.tip: Clarify immediately and without defensiveness: the Trinity is not three gods and never included Mary — one God, and you can often watch genuine surprise register.

aboutyou.t: You are 'People of the Book' — honored and superseded
aboutyou.d: The Quran grants Christians a special status (Ahl al-Kitab): Muslims may eat your food and marry your women, and Quran 5:82 calls Christians 'nearest in affection' to believers. But the frame is supersession — your revelation was true for its time and has been corrected and replaced by Islam, much as Christians view the Mosaic covenant.
aboutyou.tip: Receive the respect and understand its shape: your friend honors you as holding an expired version of the truth, which is why 'we both follow Abraham's God' warms the room but never closes the distance by itself.

aboutyou.t: They were taught your Bible is corrupted — before they could read
aboutyou.d: The doctrine of tahrif holds that Jews and Christians altered their scriptures (citing Quran 2:79 and similar verses), so the Bible is unreliable except where the Quran confirms it. It's absorbed in childhood as background fact, though classical scholars actually disagreed on whether the corruption was of the text or only its interpretation.
aboutyou.tip: Gently ask which verse says the text was corrupted, and note the Quran itself tells Christians to judge by the Gospel (5:47) and says none can change God's words (6:115) — a door the quran-affirms-torah-gospel case walks through.

aboutyou.t: A verse warns against taking you as an intimate ally
aboutyou.d: Quran 5:51 says 'do not take the Jews and the Christians as awliya' — a word meaning allies/protectors, which some communities absorb as a caution against close friendship, though mainstream scholars (following Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari) limit it to wartime political alliances, noting the Quran elsewhere permits marriage to Christian women. Teaching on it ranges from strict to warmly open.
aboutyou.tip: Don't take initial guardedness personally; consistent, agenda-free friendship is precisely the evidence that dissolves the suspicious reading.

aboutyou.t: They believe you were born Muslim
aboutyou.d: Per hadith (Bukhari 1358), every child is born on the fitra — the natural disposition toward Islam — 'and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian.' This is why converts to Islam are called 'reverts': your Christianity is seen as a parental overlay on your true factory settings.
aboutyou.tip: Knowing this reframes the conversation: to them you're not choosing between religions but returning home or staying estranged — so your testimony of actually meeting God in Christ confronts the theory with a person.

aboutyou.t: Christian morality is judged by the culture's fruits
aboutyou.d: Many Muslims are taught to read Western drinking, dating, immodesty, and family breakdown as Christianity's produce — since the West is assumed to be 'Christian,' Hollywood becomes your Sunday school. A devout Muslim may sincerely believe their moral standards exceed yours.
aboutyou.tip: A visibly holy life — sexual integrity, sobriety, honored parents, generosity — dismantles this teaching more powerfully than any argument, and distinguishing 'Western' from 'Christian' out loud helps.

aboutyou.t: Missionaries are pre-cast as colonial agents
aboutyou.d: Christian missions arrived in much of the Muslim world alongside European empires — under British rule in Egypt, French rule in Algeria — and are remembered as imperialism's soft arm; many Muslim-majority states restricted missionaries at independence. 'Evangelism' can therefore register as geopolitical aggression, not good news.
aboutyou.tip: Be transparently a friend, not a project with a timeline — Muslims can smell a target-based friendship, and the accusation collapses when your love visibly doesn't depend on their conversion.

aboutyou.t: Questioning Islam carries costs you've never paid
aboutyou.d: Leaving Islam is criminalized in some 23 countries (13 with capital statutes), and even in the West an ex-Muslim commonly risks family rupture, ostracism, and lost marriages — honor and religion are fused, so a child's doubt shames the whole family. Your friend's hesitancy to engage hard questions may be fear of the price, not lack of interest.
aboutyou.tip: Never push for public declarations; offer private space, absolute discretion, and count the cost with them — Luke 14 realism honors what following Jesus would actually require of them.

aboutyou.d: Muslims revere Isa as a major prophet: virgin-born, sinless in most tellings, a miracle-worker who healed lepers and raised the dead by God's permission, the Messiah who will return — named 25 times in the Quran, more than Muhammad. Speaking ill of Jesus genuinely offends a Muslim.
aboutyou.tip: Start where the love already is: 'tell me what you believe about Jesus' opens warmly, and 'why would God's Messiah matter this much?' lets his actual words in the Gospels do the rest.

aboutyou.t: Sunni and Shia: a succession crisis at the very start
aboutyou.d: Islam split within a generation of Muhammad's death (632 AD) over who should lead: Abu Bakr, chosen by the community (the Sunni position), or Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, designated by divine right (the Shia position). Karbala (680) sealed the divide in blood. Today roughly 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10-15% Shia, concentrated in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, and Lebanon. Twelver Shia — the large majority of Shia — hold that the twelfth imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, entered hiding ('occultation') in 874 AD, is still alive, and will return as the Mahdi to bring justice.
aboutyou.tip: Never assume which tradition your friend belongs to — ask, and ask what it means to them; Shia friends especially may carry a strong sense of historical grievance and love for the Prophet's family. The split itself can open honest conversation: if God's final revelation left no clear successor and the community fractured immediately, what does that say about where authority really lies? Christians can point to a Shepherd who said his sheep hear his voice — and who never left.

aboutyou.t: Sufism: the mystical hunger inside Islam
aboutyou.d: Sufism is Islam's mystical stream — the whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi order (Rumi's heirs), dhikr chanting, saint veneration, and shrine pilgrimage. For centuries it was mainstream piety across much of the Muslim world, and it remains woven through South Asian, Turkish, and African Islam. Salafis and Wahhabis condemn shrine visitation and saint intercession as shirk (idolatry) — which is why jihadist and Salafi movements bulldoze Sufi shrines (Timbuktu 2012, ISIS across Iraq and Syria, the 2017 massacre of 300+ worshippers at a Sufi mosque in Sinai). The battle over Sufism is an intra-Islamic war about whether God can be intimately experienced.
aboutyou.tip: A Sufi-inclined friend is telling you something precious: they hunger for closeness to God, not just rule-keeping — and their own tradition's hardliners call that hunger idolatry. Don't debate; resonate. Share what union with God looks like in Christ: 'Abide in me' (John 15), the indwelling Spirit, adoption as sons. The longing Sufism reaches for through techniques and saints, the gospel offers as a gift and a certainty.

aboutyou.t: Hafiz culture: memorized sound vs. studied meaning
aboutyou.d: A hafiz is someone who has memorized the entire Quran in Arabic — all 6,000+ verses — and Muslim communities worldwide produce millions of them, often children. But since roughly 80% of Muslims are not native Arabic speakers, many huffaz can recite the whole book flawlessly without understanding the language. This isn't seen as a deficiency: in Islam the Quran IS the Arabic recitation — the sound itself is the sacred object, and reward attaches to recitation per letter. Translations are officially only 'interpretations of the meanings.' Christians relate to scripture almost oppositely: the Bible is meaning meant to be translated, studied, and understood, in every language from the start (Acts 2).
aboutyou.tip: Never belittle memorization — it reflects real devotion and discipline that puts most Christians' scripture engagement to shame; say so. Instead, ask meaning questions with genuine curiosity: 'That surah you recited — what is it saying? What does it mean to you?' Then offer to read a Gospel together in your friend's heart language. The experience of scripture that speaks directly, in their own tongue, about a God who wants to be understood, is often itself the door.
